summary: git rebase moves your branch so it starts from the newest commit of another branch. The result is a straight history with no merge commit.
notes: Rebase copies each commit onto the new base, so every copied commit gets a new hash.
If a replayed commit conflicts, fix the file, git add it, and run git rebase --continue. git rebase --abort cancels.
Merge keeps the history exactly as it happened. Rebase rewrites it to look like you started later. Both end with the same files.
pitfall: Do not rebase commits you already pushed and others pulled. Their copies have the old hashes, and the next pull mixes both versions. Rebase only local work.
setup_note: Starts on main. The branch letter-grades has two commits, and main got one more commit after the branch started.
setup:
cat > gradebook.py <<'EOF'
scores = [88, 92, 79, 95]
average = sum(scores) / len(scores)
print("Average:", average)
EOF

cat > README.md <<'EOF'
# Gradebook
Quiz socres for Period 3.
EOF
git add -A && git commit -q -m "Add gradebook script"

cat > scores.csv <<'EOF'
name,score
Ava,88
Liam,92
Noah,79
Zoe,95
EOF
git add -A && git commit -q -m "Add quiz scores"

printf '%s' 'def letter(score):
    return "A" if score >= 90 else "B"
' >> gradebook.py
git add -A && git commit -q -m "Add letter grade function"
git add -A && git commit -q -m "Print the letter grade"
git add -A && git commit -q -m "Fix typo in README"
